questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14041137/assets/816c4ecbfe49321bc6b2bc0d72eb61d6ddd1aeae7e76a275df0975439dde5865.png)

Consider the picture above. Given that $c=a+\lambda b,$ find $\lambda .$
questions.worked_solution:
To find $\lambda ,$ we want to match the expression

$$
c=a+\lambda b.
$$

We are given that one of the components is $a.$ So, we begin with the vector $a,$ and then find the remaining vector needed to reach the point $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14041137/assets/6782f2fa59056afd9022edbaf69c44a991bf12a7ac6a190bea3cc08fc7a4996c.png)

Note that in $△OAC,$ we have:

- $AC=2.5|b|$

- $\overset{\to }{AC}$ and $b$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overset{\to }{AC}=2.5b.$

Additionally,

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AC} \\  & =a+2.5b.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=a+\lambda b=a+2.5b.$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $b,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =2.5
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14041137/assets/36742531a5f9f5d77c5f7e90980120479f4142cecaf6e84937d76d938688409d.png)

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OM}=d,$ $\overset{\to }{ON}=e,$ and $T$ divides $\overset{―}{MN}$ in the ratio $MT:TN=8:3.$ Express $\overset{\to }{OT}$ via the vectors $d$ and $e.$

$\,\overset{\to }{OT}=$
{{field-1}}
$d+$
{{field-2}}
$e$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OT}=\overset{\to }{OM}+\overset{\to }{MT}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OM}=d,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{MT}.$

First, from $△OMN,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{MN} & =\overset{\to }{MO}+\overset{\to }{ON} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OM}+\overset{\to }{ON} \\  & =-d+e \\  & =e-d.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $MT:TN=8:3,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{MT}=\frac{8}{11}\overset{\to }{MN}=\frac{8}{11}(e-d).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OT} & =\overset{\to }{OM}+\overset{\to }{MT} \\  & =d+\frac{8}{11}(e-d) \\  & =\frac{3}{11}d+\frac{8}{11}e.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OD}=d,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{DF}.$

First, from $△ODE,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{DE} & =\overset{\to }{DO}+\overset{\to }{OE} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OD}+\overset{\to }{OE} \\  & =-d+e \\  & =e-d.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $DF:FE=3:4,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{DF}=\frac{3}{7}\overset{\to }{DE}=\frac{3}{7}(e-d).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OF} & =\overset{\to }{OD}+\overset{\to }{DF} \\  & =d+\frac{3}{7}(e-d) \\  & =\frac{4}{7}d+\frac{3}{7}e.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Two Scalar Factors in a Linear Combination
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the picture below. Given that $\mathbf{m}=\lambda\mathbf{n}+\mu\mathbf{k}$, find $\lambda$ and $\mu$.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14041137/assets/b8abf22d14f93a38c4d01f368b8171e4ccfe90086d932f5b58453baa46391405.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14041137/assets/76b9867a7c1ef484922241ebe44272f0104e406c31310bf36227a13850f50d8b.png)

In $\bigtriangleup ONM$ shown above, we have:

- $ON=2|\mathbf{n}|$;

- $\overrightarrow{ON}$ and $\mathbf{n}$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overrightarrow{ON}=2\mathbf{n}$.

Similarly:

- $NM=2|\mathbf{k}|$

- $\overrightarrow{NM}$ and $\mathbf{k}$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overrightarrow{NM}=2\mathbf{k}$.

Additionally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\overset{\to }{ON}+\overset{\to }{NM} \\  & =2n+2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $\mathbf{m}=\lambda\mathbf{n}+\mu\mathbf{k}=2\mathbf{n}+2\mathbf{k}$. 

Since $\mathbf{n} \nparallel \mathbf{k},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{n}$ and $\mathbf{k}$, we get:

- $\lambda=2$ and $\mu=2$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Vector That Satisfies a Ratio in Terms of Known Vectors
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following diagram, where $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a},$ $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf{b},$ and $X$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $3:1.$ Find $\overrightarrow{OX}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14041137/assets/678ea2936b8a5b1ded74cb8a0875c629e8be0f7002c98492ebf2e8109fc603ef.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overrightarrow{OX} = \overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AX}.
$$

We're told that $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a},$ so we just need to work out $\overrightarrow{AX}.$

First, from $\triangle OAB,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $AX:XB=3:1,$ we have

$$
\overrightarrow{AX}=\dfrac{3}{4}\overrightarrow{AB}=\dfrac{3}{4}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OX} & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AX} \\  & =a+\frac{3}{4}(b-a) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}a+\frac{3}{4}b.\end{aligned}
$$
